before: Inheritance lets a derived class reuse accessible members of a base class. class TimedTask : StudyTask declares StudyTask as the direct base.
A TimedTask instance contains the inherited state and its own added state. Public base members are accessible through it. A class has at most one direct base class.
A TimedTask reference can be stored in a StudyTask variable. Both references still refer to the same object. The declared StudyTask type does not expose Minutes, which only the derived type declares.
Expected behavior from this example: 7 then 20. This expected result is a reasoned prediction until a compiler test is recorded.

Optional local transfer task: Add a public base method that increases Score, then call it through the derived object. Use a .NET 10 console project with C# 14; reading completion does not verify this local work.
after: Inheritance lets one class build on another. The existing class is the base class. The new class is the derived class. TimedTask : StudyTask means TimedTask builds on StudyTask.
A TimedTask object has the inherited Score field and its own Minutes field. A C# class can have only one direct base class.
A TimedTask can be stored in a StudyTask variable. This copies a reference to the same object, not a separate object.
The program prints 7, then 20. general changes the same object's Score. Minutes stays unchanged.
general is declared as StudyTask, so that name exposes the base class's members. It cannot directly access Minutes, even though the actual object is a TimedTask.

before.question: Assign general.Score = 9 instead. Which two values print through timed?
before.explanation: The base-typed variable general refers to the same TimedTask object. Its inherited Score changes; Minutes is a separate field and remains 20.
